doc.title: Orrin Keepnews interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Francisco, California, August 7, 2002

title: Budgets and union scale in the late 1950s
summary: He gives scale of $41.25 and a trio record cost of about $500, and says small companies could then start without capital.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Royalties, publishing and who owns the song

blocks.x: What was the typical budget? I don’t know if you can say typical?

You can’t do that for several reasons. One reason you can’t do that is that I’m talking now basically late 50s, early 60s, the value of the dollar is so outrageously different that you can’t make comparisons. Even if you allow for this, that or the other, you lose all sense of — I mean there were no journeymen ball players making over a million dollars a year in those days, just to take an example of the world of entertainment and how things have changed. Also another thing I like to point out was that now there’s a lot, because like I say everything was a lot cheaper but it didn’t really mean that much because the standard of living was different, everything cost less, but what it really boils down to is you got paid less for things. It was fourteen cents for a loaf of bread or whatever, but the fact of the matter is when you get down to the irreducible minimum and it’s still dollars that are being paid, the difference is important, so that it is relevant to point out that union scale for a musician recording, a sideman doing three hours of work in which fifteen minutes of music for an album could be created, scale was $41.25. Now that was not outrageously bad but it just — what is scale today?
I don’t know anymore. It’s a lot more than that.

Well the scale today is several hundred dollars. So that whatever, and I must confess I should know better but I’ve gotten to the point where the reason I’m not — I mean I still do a certain amount of recording but I’ve gotten into the habit where you pay sidemen a lump sum that is never going to be as small as what scale is so I mean I don’t even deal in terms of thinking about things that way. Nevertheless the whole point is that we did records very economically. Let’s put it that way. The fact is that you could do a trio record and your musicians costs might total $500. You know you might roughly speaking be paying $125 to each sideman and $250 to the leader and that’s probably what got paid on the first Bill Evans album. And nothing — nobody was exploiting anybody. It also meant that even though the record only sold 800 copies in the first year, so we didn’t come out ahead on it, but it was not unthinkable to say let’s continue working with this guy. Because he deserves to be recorded. So you can’t — and I do absolutely refuse to try and translate — it would take, maybe if I got on somebody’s program sometime in the presence of let’s say a jazz fan who was also a significant economist, we could have a discussion about that, and I’d love to do that sometime. Unfortunately I’ve never ever come across such a person. I would love to talk with such a person and it certainly should be, by all means, should be a public conversation — a lot of people — I would love to know more myself about what that relationship is. What I do know is this, I know it was possible to make jazz records without having any significant or even noticeable amount of capitalization. That’s the important fact.
